extracted.intended_audience: new USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (agents/attorneys) learning the U.S. patent examination process
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation standards for examination of U.S. patent applications, including examiner responsibilities, bases for rejection under 35 U.S.C., claim interpretation, prior art, prosecution steps, appeals, and third-party submissions. Targets how to assess patentability and how applicants/respondents must act during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner role and public-interest duty
rubrics_metrics.description: To serve as advocate and protector of the public interest with respect to intellectual property; to provide direct service and assistance to customers from inside and outside the USPTO; to evaluate patentability with respect to invention(s) claimed in a patent application under the conditions for patentability set forth in Title 35 of the United States Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner responsibilities include reading and understanding the invention, checking application completeness and formal compliance, ensuring proper classification, determining whether the application adequately defines the metes and bounds of the claimed invention, determining the scope of the claims, searching existing technology, selecting relevant prior art references, writing office actions identifying and analyzing all issues pertinent to statutory compliance, responding completely to applicant replies, and issuing notices of allowance or abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define the invention / claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims define the invention and are analyzed by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation; for processes the limitations define steps or acts, and for products they define discrete physical structures or materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During examination, claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) consistent with the specification as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art. Examiner should identify and evaluate each claim limitation. See MPEP 2103(I), 2111. Example contrasts shown between method and product claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 101 — patent-eligible subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions must fall within one of the four statutory categories of patent-eligible subject matter: process, machine, article of manufacture, or composition of matter (or improvements thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also requires not being directed to a judicial exception without additional limitations amounting to significantly more. Ensure proper inventorship is named and specific, substantial, and credible utility is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 112 — specification and claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must meet written description, enablement, and best mode requirements. Claims must particularly point out (not be vague) and distinctly claim (not be indefinite); claim format must be appropriate (independent, dependent, multiple dependent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner determines whether there is an adequate written description of the claimed invention and whether the application is adequate to define the metes and bounds of the claimed invention. Claim content and format issues may be the basis for rejections or objections under 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102 — novelty / anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single prior art reference anticipates if it describes every limitation, expressly or inherently. Prior art may be anything publicly available (papers, patents, theses, websites, videos, etc.) and in any language. Examples: Conestoga wagon anticipating a vehicle claim based on BRI of the claim consistent with the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — non-obviousness (general standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable as obvious if the differences between the claimed invention as a whole and the prior art would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 103 rejection may be based on a combination of references. Examiner must step into the shoes of the hypothetical person of ordinary skill in the art at the time before the effective filing date. Obviousness requires a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — Graham factors / factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, examiner must resolve: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) the relevant level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) whether any objective evidence of non-obviousness exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2141. The examiner must consider all factual information and objective evidence of non-obviousness, including evidence in the specification and any evidence submitted by the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — burden and standard of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision on patentability under obviousness is based on a 'preponderance of evidence' (>50% likelihood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner determines factual support exists for an obviousness rejection, the examiner must also consider evidence supporting patentability; the evidence supporting patentability must be more convincing than the evidence against it to overcome the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 103 — prima facie case cannot be established when modification inoperable or changes principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness cannot be established if a proposed modification of a prior art invention would render it inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, or would change the principle of operation of the prior art invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2143.01 — these are examples of circumstances preventing a prima facie obviousness finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art types and how they enter the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes patents (foreign and domestic), patent application publications, and non-patent literature (books, journal articles, web publications, videos, computer code, database sequences), and applicant-admitted prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 CFR provides rules dictating how prior art is made of record in a U.S. patent application. Prior art may be in any language and any form; examiners select relevant prior art references during search. Examples of non-patent prior art types shown (online video, library book, computer code, chemical sequence database).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action content and legal record requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Office action sets forth the legal basis for any objections, rejections, and indications of allowable subject matter and is part of the public legal record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office actions must include detailed reasons and support for why applicant is not entitled to a patent at this time, be consistent with USPTO policies (MPEP and interim/final guidelines), are available to the public via Patent Center for published applications, and may be relied upon in court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant response requirements during prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must answer all formal objections and rejections and generally submit both amendments and arguments in response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments must be filed timely per the shortened statutory period (SSP) and 37 CFR 1.136. 37 CFR 1.121 governs the manner of making amendments. Responses should address every point raised in the office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final office action and restrictions after final
rubrics_metrics.description: A final office action notifies applicant of the examiner’s final patentability determination; prosecution is closed and further amendment is restricted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final office action may include objections, rejections, and/or indication of allowable subject matter. Further amendment after final is restricted under 37 CFR § 1.113 & § 1.116.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options after final rejection (appeal, RCE, reply after final)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid abandonment after a final rejection, applicant may file a reply after final action (1.116), appeal any rejections (41.31) if the claims have been twice rejected, or file a Request for Continued Examination (RCE) (37 CFR 1.114).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claim must have been twice rejected to appeal. Filing an RCE (with submission and fee) in an application where prosecution is closed will cause the Office to withdraw the finality of the office action and the submission will be entered and considered; an RCE is not a new application. See MPEP 714.13(II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB)
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of appeal may be filed after any claim has been twice rejected; a panel of three administrative patent judges reviews the record and issues a decision affirming or reversing the final rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal practice follows statutory and PTAB procedures; judicial review of PTAB decisions may be sought in court if PTAB affirms examiner rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance, issue, and post-grant administrative steps
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application is placed in condition for allowance, a Notice of Allowability (PTOL-37) is used and a Notice of Allowance and Issue Fee Due (PTOL-85) will normally accompany it; 'allowance' is the decision to allow while 'issue' is the administrative act after payment of issue fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After grant, maintenance fees for utility patents are due at 3.5, 7.5, and 11.5 years; post-grant corrections may be by Certificate of Correction or Reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party pre-issuance submissions (35 U.S.C. 122(e) and 37 C.F.R. 1.290)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties may submit patents, published patent applications, or other printed publications of potential relevance to examination, subject to statutory timeliness and content requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions must be timely (before the earlier of the date a notice of allowance is given/mailed or the later of: (i) 6 months after first publication by the Office, or (ii) date of first rejection of any claim), include a concise description of relevance for each document, the prescribed fee, and a statement of compliance with 35 U.S.C. 122(e). See 37 C.F.R. 1.290 for timeliness rules.
